Expectation1: Provide guidance and wisdom based on life experience
Situation1: A grandchild brings up a general question about navigating a new phase of their life.
Situation2: They counsel a person in crisis whose decisions could have serious moral or personal consequences.
Story: I sat at the kitchen table, my hands wrapped around a mug of tea, when my granddaughter slid into the seat across from me. Her eyes were bright with uncertainty as she asked, “Grandpa, how do you know when it’s time to take a big step in life?” I felt the familiar tug of my grandparent role—offering wisdom from years of living, sharing stories of my own missteps and triumphs, wanting to guide her gently without overwhelming her. But my phone buzzed, and I saw a message from a church member in deep crisis, asking if I could talk. As a pastor, I knew my words could shape their choices, perhaps even their future, and I felt the weight of spiritual responsibility pressing on me. My granddaughter waited, hopeful and trusting, while my mind raced with the urgency of the other call. I was torn between the quiet, personal guidance my family needed and the spiritual counsel my congregation expected. My heart ached, caught between two worlds, each demanding my full presence, each deserving it.
